issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' is an avoidance/safety behaviour rather than a threat appraisal item. In this profile, the Threat node otherwise contains felt current danger and reliving; this item is misclassified and weakens within-node coherence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is not phrased as a strategy and appears to describe a trigger category. It is also weakly supported by the rest of the profile, since no memory, threat, or appraisal content specifically involves authorities or uniforms. This creates a cross-node mismatch and a node-level inconsistency within Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Fatima is a 55-year-old divorced woman of Iraqi origin who works as an HVAC technician in the Phoenix metropolitan area. She came to the United States as a refugee more than two decades ago, and for many years she managed to build a life that felt, if not entirely safe, at least functional. She raised her children, learned a trade, and kept moving. It was only in the past year, after a combination of personal losses and an unexpected environmental trigger, that the architecture of that coping finally began to give way. She presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 63, describing a life increasingly organized around fear she could neither name cleanly nor escape entirely.

The events Fatima fled unfolded over several weeks during a period of violent civil unrest in her home region. She was among a group of civilians attempting to cross into a neighboring country through a route that took them along a swollen river. The crossing was made at night, in near-total silence enforced by the group's guides, who warned that any sound could draw attention. At one point the makeshift raft they were using began to take on water. Fatima, who could not swim, felt the cold press of the river against her legs, then her waist, and then the rough, waterlogged rope she gripped with both hands as the raft tilted. The texture of that rope - fibrous, wet, fraying - was the last thing she was certain of before the chaos that followed. Several people were lost. She survived. She does not fully understand how.

For years afterward, Fatima described functioning through a kind of willed amnesia. She worked long hours in residential and commercial buildings, focused on ductwork and refrigerant lines and the satisfying logic of mechanical systems. But the memory had not gone anywhere. When it returned - in dreams, in unguarded moments - it arrived with a force so disproportionate to ordinary life that she had come to believe it could not really have happened to her. The events felt like something she had witnessed rather than survived, and yet the shame that accompanied them was entirely her own. She found herself wondering, in ways she could not fully articulate, whether she had done something wrong in surviving, whether her stillness during the crossing had cost someone else their life. When the memory surfaced fully, the emotional weight was so immediate and total that she had learned to abort the recall - to stand up, walk out of a room, run water, do anything that interrupted the return of it.

In her work, Fatima regularly enters mechanical rooms, crawl spaces, and utility areas - environments that are often silent in a particular way, a pressurized quiet that precedes the hum of a system coming online. She had come to dread that silence. In those moments before a unit kicked on, she was certain something was about to go wrong, that the stillness meant danger was organizing itself just outside her awareness. She had developed a habit, which she described almost apologetically, of identifying the exit before she touched a single tool. In larger commercial buildings she sometimes walked the perimeter of a space before beginning work, not inspecting equipment but mapping ways out. Colleagues had noticed. A supervisor had asked, twice now, whether she was all right.

Water presented its own difficulty. Phoenix flooded rarely, but monsoon season brought arroyos running brown and fast, and there had been a job site near a retention pond where she had stood at the edge of the parking lot and been unable to walk closer. She told the client she needed to retrieve a part. She drove away and did not return. She lost that contract.

Rope, or anything with a similar coarse, braided texture - certain gloves, some types of insulation wrap - she handled as little as possible and never without registering it. She could not explain this to anyone.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was her youngest daughter's wedding, approaching in the spring, to be held near a lake. She had not told her daughter about her fear. What she most hoped for, she said quietly in the intake session, was to be present for that day. What she most feared was that she would not be able to make herself stay.
